q: `saved` is `{ volume: 0, shuffle: false, name: "" }`. Which expressions keep the user's saved value instead of the default? Select all that apply.
explain: `??` only falls back when the left side is `undefined` or `null`, so `0` and `false` are kept. `||` falls back on any **falsy** value, so `0 || 50` gives `50` and `"" || "Untitled"` gives `"Untitled"`. Sometimes that's what you want for an empty name, but it isn't "keeping the saved value".

q: A teammate merges saved settings over the defaults. What is `b`?
explain: Spread copies properties left to right, and **later wins**. `volume` is first set to 20 from `saved`, then overwritten with 50 from `defaults`, so the user's choice is lost. An object can't hold the same key twice; the last write is the value. Defaults go first, overrides last: `{ ...defaults, ...saved }` gives `{ volume: 20, shuffle: false }`.

q: Why is the last line a compile error?
options: Optional properties can't be read, only written
Interfaces can't have optional properties; that needs `type`
explain: `rating?: number` means the property may be missing, so reading it gives `number | undefined`. TypeScript won't pass a maybe-`undefined` into a parameter that needs a `number`. Fix it at the point of use: `"★".repeat(t.rating ?? 0)`. `?` doesn't create a default value, and both `interface` and `type` support optional properties.

q: A playlist editor shows the new track in the *old* playlist too. Which line is the bug?
options: Line 2: the spread copy shares the same `tracks` array, so `push` changes the original
Line 1: spread doesn't copy anything, `copy` is `p`
None, `push` on a copy is always safe
explain: Spread is **shallow**. `copy` is a new object, so changing `copy.name` wouldn't affect `p`. But `copy.tracks` is the same array as `p.tracks`, and `push` modifies that shared array. Build a new array instead: `return { ...p, tracks: [...p.tracks, t] };`.

q: Which of these can you write with `type` but **not** with `interface`? Select all that apply.
options: An object shape `{ id: number; title: string }`
A shape that has everything another shape has, plus one field
explain: An interface always describes an object shape, so unions like `"small" | "medium"` or `number | string` need a `type` alias. Plain object shapes work with both. Extending works with both too: `interface B extends A { … }` or `type B = A & { … }`.
